name: chem-r5
context:
Round 5 on a chemistry layer for a dice puzzle game. A MEASUREMENT HAS FALSIFIED THE FEATURE'S CENTRAL CLAIM and this brief proposes the fix. Review the fix, not the old design.

WHAT FAILED. The board held FREE ATOMS. A player selected a connected region, the game solved bond orders so every valence was exact, checked the shape against a library of real molecules, and scored the energy released — which, from free atoms, is the sum of the bonds formed. We then measured whether understanding chemistry actually pays, over 400 paired rounds of 12 turns, comparing four policies: 'random' (takes any legal move), 'biggest' (takes the move with the most atoms — the match-3 instinct, requiring no chemistry), 'valence' (takes the move with greatest total valence — grasps 'more bonds means more energy', memorises nothing), and 'energy' (takes the highest-energy move — the full bond-enthalpy table).

Results: valence beat biggest by only +1.43% at t=1.23, losing or tying on 276 of 400 boards. 'energy' beat 'valence' by 0.01% at t=0.04. Meanwhile 'biggest' beat 'random' by +8.37% at t=4.13. Correlation between atom count and energy over 592 real moves: r = 0.843. So 84% of the score is explained by how many tiles you cleared, 'bigger is better' is near-optimal, and chemical understanding is worth nothing measurable. The chemistry is currently a costume.

The cause is structural: building from free atoms BREAKS no bonds, so the score is a sum over bonds formed, which grows with atom count. Only a reaction, where bonds break as well as form, can decouple energy from size.

THE PROPOSED FIX. Board tiles become MOLECULES rather than free atoms, drawn from the same 16-molecule library (H2, O2, N2, H2O, CH4, CO2, NH3, HCN, C2H2, H2O2, CH2O, CH3Cl, HF, HCl, F2, Cl2). A move selects a connected region of two or more molecule tiles. The game pools their atoms, then searches for the multiset of library molecules whose atom counts exactly equal that pool — CONSERVATION OF MASS as a hard constraint — and picks the product set maximising energy released, which is delta-H reversed: sum(bonds formed) minus sum(bonds broken). Products replace the reactants on the board. The player sees the balanced equation the game derived.

The intended consequence is that size stops predicting score. Methane plus two oxygens releases 808 kJ/mol. Nitrogen is a large, high-energy molecule that is nearly useless as a reactant precisely because breaking its 941 kJ/mol triple bond costs more than most rearrangements can repay, so a big tile can be a LIABILITY. The skill becomes choosing which molecules to combine, and the thing learned is which combinations release energy and why.

questions.text: Will reaction scoring actually decouple score from the number of tiles cleared, or will a new size proxy simply emerge and leave the claim just as false?
Having the game solve for the best product set means the player never balances an equation themselves. Does that destroy the learning, or is choosing the reactants the real skill?
What is the strongest reason a player would find 'select molecules, game computes products' opaque or unfair rather than educational?
Is maximising energy released the right product choice, given that real reactions are governed by kinetics and activation barriers, not only thermodynamics?
Name the specific real chemistry this proposed fix would teach WRONGLY.
